description: Critical-care nursing concepts taught from the ground up: physiology first, then monitoring and recognition, then applied scenarios. Quick questions, clear explanations. Verify clinical specifics against the AACN CCRN content outline and current references before relying on them.

questions.question: Which chamber is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle is the thick-walled bottom-left chamber (on the patient's left, so the viewer's right). It pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and out to the body — which is why it's the strongest chamber.

questions.question: Which chamber is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The right atrium is the upper chamber on the patient's right. It receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the superior and inferior vena cava and holds the SA node.

questions.question: Which structure is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The aorta is the big red vessel leaving the left ventricle. It carries oxygenated blood to the body. Its pressure is what the left ventricle's afterload is measured against.

questions.question: Which structure is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs — the one artery in the body that carries blue blood. A PA catheter sits here.

questions.question: Which chamber is highlighted?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle is the lower chamber on the patient's right. It pumps into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation, so its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's.

questions.question: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by what?
questions.explanation: CO = HR × SV. Stroke volume is the blood ejected per beat, so beats per minute × volume per beat gives volume per minute.

questions.question: Preload is best described as:
choices: The resistance the ventricle pumps against
The stretch on the ventricle at the end of filling
questions.explanation: Preload is end-diastolic volume — how full and stretched the ventricle is before it contracts. More preload generally means more stretch and (up to a point) a stronger beat.

questions.question: Afterload is best described as:
choices: The volume in the ventricle before contraction
The resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood
The amount of blood returning to the heart
questions.explanation: Afterload is the pressure/resistance the ventricle pushes against to open the valve and eject. High afterload (e.g., vasoconstriction, aortic stenosis) makes the heart work harder.

questions.question: Contractility refers to:
choices: The intrinsic strength of the heart muscle's squeeze
questions.explanation: Contractility is how forcefully the myocardium contracts independent of preload or afterload. Drugs like dobutamine raise it; ischemia and acidosis lower it.

questions.question: The Frank–Starling principle says that, up to a limit, more stretch on the ventricle leads to:
questions.explanation: Within physiologic limits, more end-diastolic stretch produces a more forceful ejection — which is why giving fluid (raising preload) can raise stroke volume.

questions.question: Which structure is the heart's normal pacemaker?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node fires fastest, so it sets the rhythm. The AV node and ventricles have slower backup rates that only take over if the SA node fails.

questions.question: The P wave on an ECG represents:
questions.explanation: The P wave is the atria depolarizing (electrically activating) before they contract. Ventricular depolarization is the QRS; ventricular repolarization is the T wave.

questions.question: The PR interval measures the time from:
choices: Start of atrial activation to start of ventricular activation
Start to end of ventricular activation
questions.explanation: PR runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS — mostly the delay at the AV node. A long PR means conduction through the AV node is slow (first-degree block).

questions.question: Why does the AV node deliberately slow the impulse?
choices: To speed up the heart rate
To let the atria finish filling the ventricles
questions.explanation: The AV delay gives the atria time to contract and top off the ventricles (the 'atrial kick') before the ventricles fire. Losing that kick, as in atrial fibrillation, can drop cardiac output.

questions.question: What does the highlighted wave represent?
questions.explanation: The small first bump is the P wave: the atria depolarizing. Every normal beat starts here, triggered by the SA node.

questions.question: What does the highlighted complex represent?
questions.explanation: The tall sharp spike is the QRS: the ventricles depolarizing. A narrow QRS means the impulse used the normal fast conduction system; a wide one means it didn't.

questions.question: What does the highlighted wave represent?
questions.explanation: The rounded bump after the QRS is the T wave: the ventricles recharging (repolarizing). Peaked T waves hint at hyperkalemia; the ST segment just before it is where ischemia shows.

questions.question: The highlighted span, from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS, is the:
questions.explanation: The PR interval is mostly the AV node's built-in delay. When it stretches beyond about 0.20 seconds (one big box), that's first-degree AV block.

questions.question: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is a measure of:
choices: Average pressure driving blood into the organs
questions.explanation: MAP is the average arterial pressure over a cardiac cycle and the best single number for organ perfusion. A common goal in shock is a MAP of about 65 mmHg or more.

questions.question: Central venous pressure (CVP) is used as a rough estimate of:
questions.explanation: CVP reflects pressure in the right atrium, which approximates right ventricular filling (preload). It's an imperfect estimate, which is why trends matter more than one value.

questions.question: Pulmonary artery occlusion (wedge) pressure estimates:
questions.explanation: When the PA catheter balloon is inflated, it reads 'through' the pulmonary circulation to the left atrium, approximating left ventricular filling pressure.

questions.question: Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is the hemodynamic number for:
questions.explanation: SVR is the resistance in the systemic arteries that the left ventricle pumps against — the measured version of afterload. Vasodilation lowers it; vasoconstriction raises it.

questions.question: A low mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) usually means:
choices: Tissues are extracting more oxygen than normal — delivery is not keeping up with demand
questions.explanation: SvO2 is the oxygen left in blood after it passes the tissues. When delivery falls (low output, low Hgb, low SaO2) or demand rises, tissues pull more oxygen out and SvO2 drops.

questions.question: 'Reentry' as a cause of arrhythmia means:
choices: The SA node fires too fast
An impulse circles back and re-stimulates tissue that has already recovered
questions.explanation: Reentry is an electrical loop: a wave of activation travels around a circuit and keeps re-exciting tissue. It underlies many tachycardias, including atrial flutter and many ventricular tachycardias.

questions.question: 'Enhanced automaticity' means:
choices: Cells outside the SA node start firing on their own
Conduction is blocked at the AV node
questions.explanation: Automaticity is the ability to self-fire. When ischemia, catecholamines, or electrolyte shifts make other cells fire faster than the SA node, they take over — producing ectopic beats or rhythms.

questions.question: A 'heart block' is fundamentally a problem of:
questions.explanation: In heart block the impulse forms normally but is delayed or stopped on its way through the AV node or bundle branches. The degree of block describes how much gets through.

questions.question: Which electrolyte disturbance most classically makes the heart irritable and prone to arrhythmias?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemia makes cardiac cells more excitable and is a common, reversible cause of ectopy and ventricular arrhythmias. Low magnesium does the same and often travels with it.

questions.question: An irregularly irregular rhythm with no clear P waves is most likely:
questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver instead of contracting, so there are no organized P waves and the ventricles respond unpredictably — hence 'irregularly irregular.'

questions.question: A wide-QRS tachycardia at 180/min with no P waves is most likely:
questions.explanation: A wide QRS means the ventricles are activating abnormally (not through the normal conduction system). Fast, wide, and regular should be treated as VT until proven otherwise.

questions.question: P waves and QRS complexes marching along at their own independent rates describes:
questions.explanation: In complete block nothing gets through the AV node, so the atria and ventricles each run on their own pacemaker. The ventricular escape rate is slow and this rhythm is unstable.

questions.question: A chaotic, wavy baseline with no recognizable QRS complexes in a pulseless patient is:
questions.explanation: Ventricular fibrillation is disorganized electrical activity with no effective contraction. It produces no pulse and needs immediate defibrillation and CPR.

questions.question: A consistently prolonged PR interval with every P wave followed by a QRS is:
questions.explanation: First-degree block means every impulse gets through, just slowly. It is usually benign on its own but can be a warning sign with certain drugs or ischemia.

concepts.title: Cardiovascular: Shock as a perfusion problem

questions.question: At its core, shock is:
choices: Inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery
questions.explanation: Shock is defined by cells not getting enough oxygen, not by a single vital sign. Blood pressure can be normal early while perfusion is already failing (lactate and mental status often tell you first).

questions.question: Hypovolemic shock is primarily a problem of:
questions.explanation: Lose volume (bleeding, dehydration) and there is less blood returning to fill the heart. Less preload → less stroke volume → less output. The fix is restoring volume.

questions.question: Cardiogenic shock is primarily a problem of:
questions.explanation: The heart muscle itself can't eject enough (large MI, severe heart failure). Preload is often high, output is low, and the patient is cold and wet.

questions.question: Distributive shock (e.g., septic, anaphylactic) is primarily a problem of:
questions.explanation: The vessels dilate and leak, so the 'container' is too big for the volume in it. SVR falls, and after fluids, vasopressors are used to restore vascular tone.

questions.question: Obstructive shock means blood flow is physically blocked, as in:
choices: Cardiac tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism
questions.explanation: In tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or a large PE, the heart can't fill or eject because something is mechanically in the way. Relieving the obstruction is the treatment.

questions.question: Myocardial ischemia happens when:
choices: Oxygen supply to heart muscle can't meet its demand
questions.explanation: Ischemia is a supply/demand mismatch — usually a narrowed or blocked coronary artery. Anything that raises demand (tachycardia, hypertension) or lowers supply (hypotension, anemia) makes it worse.

questions.question: ST-segment elevation on the ECG most often signals:
choices: Full-thickness injury from a completely blocked artery
questions.explanation: ST elevation in a pattern of leads (a 'territory') indicates acute transmural injury — a STEMI — and the artery usually needs to be opened urgently.

questions.question: Troponin is useful because it:
choices: Rises when heart muscle cells are damaged
questions.explanation: Troponin is a protein inside cardiac muscle cells. When cells die it leaks into the blood, so a rising troponin confirms myocardial injury.

questions.question: The main goal of early treatment in an acute MI is to:
choices: Restore blood flow to the heart muscle quickly
Raise blood pressure as high as possible
questions.explanation: 'Time is muscle.' The faster the artery is reopened (PCI or fibrinolytics), the less heart muscle dies — which is why door-to-balloon time is tracked.

questions.question: 'Ventilation' refers to moving air in and out, and its blood-gas marker is:
questions.explanation: Ventilation clears CO2. If the lungs aren't moving enough air, CO2 builds up — so PaCO2 tells you how well the patient is ventilating.

questions.question: 'Oxygenation' refers to getting oxygen into the blood, and its markers are:
questions.explanation: PaO2 and oxygen saturation reflect oxygen uptake across the alveoli. A patient can ventilate normally yet oxygenate poorly (e.g., pneumonia), or the reverse.

questions.question: A patient breathing rapidly who still has rising CO2 is most likely:
choices: Taking breaths too shallow to clear CO2
questions.explanation: Rate alone doesn't equal ventilation; what matters is the volume reaching the alveoli each minute. Rapid shallow breathing moves mostly dead-space air, so CO2 climbs.

questions.question: Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch means:
choices: Air and blood aren't reaching the same parts of the lung
The patient is breathing too fast
The heart rate is too high
questions.explanation: Gas exchange needs air and blood to meet at the alveolus. Pneumonia (air can't get in) or pulmonary embolism (blood can't get there) both lower oxygen by mismatching the two.

questions.question: A pH below 7.35 is called:
questions.explanation: Normal arterial pH is about 7.35–7.45. Lower is acidotic, higher is alkalotic. The next step is deciding whether the lungs (CO2) or the kidneys/metabolism (bicarbonate) caused it.

questions.question: Low pH with a high PaCO2 is:
questions.explanation: CO2 is an acid. When ventilation fails and CO2 accumulates, pH drops — a respiratory acidosis. Causes include sedation, COPD exacerbation, and fatigue.

questions.question: Low pH with a low bicarbonate is:
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate is the body's base buffer. When acid builds up (lactate, ketones, kidney failure), bicarbonate is used up and pH falls — a metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: High pH with a low PaCO2 is:
questions.explanation: Blowing off CO2 removes acid, so pH rises. Hyperventilation from pain, anxiety, sepsis, or over-ventilation on a ventilator causes this.

questions.question: 'Compensation' on an ABG means:
choices: The pH has become dangerously high
The other system is shifting to pull pH back toward normal
questions.explanation: If the lungs cause an acidosis, the kidneys slowly hold onto bicarbonate; if metabolism causes it, the lungs quickly blow off CO2. Compensation moves pH toward normal but rarely fully corrects it.

questions.question: On a ventilator, which two settings most directly change CO2 removal?
questions.explanation: Rate × tidal volume = minute ventilation, which is what clears CO2. To lower PaCO2, raise the rate or the tidal volume.

questions.question: Which two settings most directly improve oxygenation?
questions.explanation: FiO2 raises the oxygen concentration delivered; PEEP keeps alveoli open at end-expiration so more surface area is available for gas exchange.

questions.question: PEEP helps oxygenation mainly by:
choices: Preventing alveoli from collapsing at the end of exhalation
questions.explanation: Positive end-expiratory pressure acts like a splint, keeping small airways and alveoli open so they stay available for oxygen exchange. Too much PEEP can reduce venous return and blood pressure.

questions.question: A sudden high-pressure alarm on a volume ventilator most likely means:
choices: The tidal volume is too low
Something is resisting the breath — secretions, biting, coughing, or a kinked tube
questions.explanation: In volume mode the ventilator pushes a set volume; if resistance rises, pressure rises. Assess the patient first (DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment).

questions.question: A low-pressure or low-volume alarm most likely means:
choices: The patient is biting the tube
questions.explanation: If pressure or returned volume drops, air is escaping somewhere — a disconnected circuit, a cuff leak, or a dislodged tube. Check the patient, then the circuit.

questions.question: In ARDS, the core lung problem is:
choices: Inflamed, leaky alveoli filling with fluid so oxygen can't cross
A blood clot in the pulmonary artery
Air trapped in the pleural space
questions.explanation: ARDS is diffuse inflammatory injury: the alveolar–capillary membrane leaks, alveoli flood and collapse, and the lungs get stiff. The hallmark is hypoxemia that doesn't respond well to extra oxygen.

questions.question: Why are ARDS patients ventilated with low tidal volumes (about 6 mL/kg ideal body weight)?
choices: To avoid over-stretching the few remaining healthy alveoli
Because the ventilator can't deliver more
questions.explanation: In ARDS only part of the lung is participating, so a normal tidal volume over-distends those alveoli and causes more injury. Small volumes are 'lung-protective.'

questions.question: Prone positioning in severe ARDS helps because it:
choices: Improves matching of ventilation and blood flow in the lungs
questions.explanation: Lying face-down shifts the heart and fluid off the dependent lung and recruits collapsed posterior alveoli, improving V/Q matching and oxygenation.

questions.question: 'Permissive hypercapnia' in ARDS means:
choices: Driving CO2 as low as possible
Accepting a higher CO2 to keep ventilation gentle
questions.explanation: Because low tidal volumes clear less CO2, clinicians accept a somewhat high PaCO2 (as long as pH is tolerable) rather than injure the lungs with bigger breaths.

questions.question: The skull holds three things — brain, blood, and CSF. If one increases, what must happen to keep pressure normal?
questions.explanation: This is the Monro–Kellie doctrine: the rigid skull has a fixed volume. Early on, CSF and venous blood shift out to compensate; once that reserve is used up, ICP climbs quickly.

questions.question: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: CPP = MAP − ICP. Blood pushes into the brain (MAP) against the pressure already inside the skull (ICP). Rising ICP or falling MAP both starve the brain.

questions.question: Which early sign suggests ICP is rising?
choices: Fixed, dilated pupils on both sides
High blood pressure with slow pulse
questions.explanation: A change in alertness or confusion is usually the first clue. Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) and blown pupils are late, ominous signs.

questions.question: Elevating the head of the bed to about 30° helps lower ICP by:
choices: Promoting venous drainage from the head
questions.explanation: Gravity helps venous blood leave the skull, reducing one of the three volumes inside. Keeping the neck midline (no kinked jugular veins) matters for the same reason.

questions.question: The Glasgow Coma Scale scores which three things?
choices: Eye opening, verbal response, motor response
questions.explanation: GCS = Eyes (1–4) + Verbal (1–5) + Motor (1–6), ranging from 3 to 15. A score of 8 or less is generally treated as coma and raises concern about airway protection.

questions.question: A single pupil that becomes large and non-reactive most likely indicates:
choices: Pressure on the third cranial nerve from swelling or herniation
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve carries the signal that constricts the pupil. Pressure on that side (expanding bleed, herniation) blocks it, so the pupil dilates and stops reacting — an emergency.

questions.question: Pinpoint pupils in an unresponsive patient should make you think of:
questions.explanation: Opioids constrict the pupils strongly. Pinpoint pupils with slow breathing is a classic opioid picture; naloxone is the reversal agent.

questions.question: Why is a change from baseline more important than any single neuro finding?
choices: Baselines don't matter in neuro patients
Trends reveal deterioration early, before late signs appear
questions.explanation: A GCS of 13 means something different in a patient who was 15 an hour ago than in one who has been 13 for days. Serial exams catch the drop in time to act.

questions.question: The two main types of stroke are:
questions.explanation: Most strokes are ischemic — a clot stops blood flow. Hemorrhagic strokes come from a ruptured vessel. The treatments are opposite, so imaging must tell them apart before anything is given.

questions.question: Why is a CT scan done before giving a clot-dissolving drug?
choices: To rule out bleeding — a thrombolytic would make a hemorrhage worse
To measure the size of the clot
To check for a brain tumor
questions.explanation: Thrombolytics dissolve clots everywhere. If the stroke is actually a bleed, the drug would be catastrophic, so a non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage comes first.

questions.question: Weakness on the right side of the body suggests the stroke is in which side of the brain?
questions.explanation: Motor pathways cross over in the brainstem, so each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. Language is also usually on the left, so right-sided weakness often comes with speech problems.

questions.question: The 'last known well' time matters because:
choices: Time-limited treatments like thrombolytics depend on it
It is needed for the GCS
questions.explanation: Reperfusion therapies have time windows measured from when the patient was last normal — not when symptoms were noticed. An unclear time can rule a patient out of treatment.

questions.question: The kidneys' filtering rate, GFR, depends heavily on:
choices: The amount of urine in the bladder
Adequate blood pressure and flow into the kidney
questions.explanation: Filtration is pressure-driven. When perfusion pressure falls (shock, hypovolemia), GFR falls and urine output drops — which is why urine output is a bedside perfusion gauge.

questions.question: A rising serum creatinine means:
choices: The kidneys are clearing less than before
questions.explanation: Creatinine is a muscle waste product cleared almost entirely by filtration. If it accumulates in the blood, filtration has dropped.

questions.question: Urine output below about 0.5 mL/kg/hour for several hours is a warning sign of:
choices: Poor kidney perfusion or acute kidney injury
questions.explanation: Oliguria is one of the earliest signs that the kidneys are under-perfused or injured. Sustained low output is part of the definition of acute kidney injury.

questions.question: Besides filtering waste, the kidneys also regulate:
questions.explanation: The kidneys adjust sodium, potassium, and water excretion and reclaim bicarbonate. When they fail, expect fluid overload, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis.

concepts.title: Renal: Acute kidney injury and electrolytes

questions.question: 'Prerenal' acute kidney injury means the problem is:
choices: Not enough blood reaching the kidney
A blockage downstream in urine flow
questions.explanation: Prerenal AKI is a perfusion problem — hypovolemia, low cardiac output, or vasodilation. The kidney itself is initially fine and recovers if flow is restored quickly.

questions.question: 'Intrarenal' (intrinsic) AKI means:
choices: The kidney tissue itself is damaged, as in acute tubular necrosis
questions.explanation: Prolonged ischemia or toxins (contrast dye, aminoglycosides) injure the tubules directly. Fixing perfusion alone won't reverse it immediately.

questions.question: 'Postrenal' AKI means:
choices: Urine flow is obstructed after the kidney
questions.explanation: Stones, an enlarged prostate, or a blocked catheter back pressure up into the kidney. Relieving the obstruction is the treatment — always check the Foley first.

questions.question: The most dangerous electrolyte consequence of kidney failure is:
choices: High potassium, which can cause lethal arrhythmias
questions.explanation: The kidneys excrete most potassium. When they fail, potassium rises; peaked T waves, widening QRS, and eventually cardiac arrest can follow. Calcium is given to protect the heart while potassium is lowered.

questions.question: On the ECG, the earliest classic sign of hyperkalemia is:
questions.explanation: High potassium speeds repolarization, producing tall narrow T waves. As it worsens, P waves flatten and the QRS widens toward a sine wave.

concepts.title: Endocrine: Glucose regulation, DKA and HHS

questions.question: Insulin's basic job is to:
choices: Move glucose from the blood into cells
questions.explanation: Insulin is the 'key' that lets cells take up glucose. Without it, sugar piles up in the blood while cells starve and switch to burning fat.

questions.question: In DKA, where do the ketones (acids) come from?
choices: Fat breakdown because cells can't use glucose
questions.explanation: With no insulin, cells burn fat instead. Fat metabolism produces ketone acids, which cause the metabolic acidosis of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.question: Why do DKA patients breathe deep and fast (Kussmaul respirations)?
choices: Because their lungs are full of fluid
To blow off CO2 and compensate for metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation: The lungs compensate for acid in the blood by removing CO2. Deep rapid breathing is the body's attempt to raise pH.

questions.question: HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state) differs from DKA mainly because:
choices: There is enough insulin to prevent ketosis, so glucose climbs much higher without acidosis
It occurs only in type 1 diabetes
questions.explanation: In HHS, a little insulin still blocks fat breakdown, so no ketoacidosis — but glucose soars, pulling water out and causing profound dehydration and altered mental status.

questions.question: As insulin is given in DKA, potassium must be watched closely because:
choices: Insulin drives potassium into cells and serum levels can crash
questions.explanation: Insulin shifts potassium into cells along with glucose. A patient whose potassium looks normal in DKA is often whole-body depleted, so it falls fast once insulin starts.

concepts.title: Endocrine: ADH, SIADH and diabetes insipidus

questions.question: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) tells the kidneys to:
questions.explanation: ADH (vasopressin) makes the collecting ducts reabsorb water, so urine becomes concentrated and the body keeps more fluid.

questions.question: In SIADH there is too much ADH, so the patient:
choices: Produces large amounts of dilute urine
Retains water and the sodium level drops (dilution)
questions.explanation: Excess ADH means water is retained, diluting the blood — low serum sodium with concentrated urine. Treatment often starts with fluid restriction.

questions.question: In diabetes insipidus there is too little ADH (or the kidney ignores it), so the patient:
choices: Produces large volumes of dilute urine and sodium rises
questions.explanation: Without ADH, the kidneys can't hold water; urine pours out dilute, and the remaining blood becomes concentrated — high sodium. It's common after pituitary surgery or severe head injury.

questions.question: Why is rapid correction of chronic low sodium dangerous?
choices: It can injure the brainstem (osmotic demyelination)
questions.explanation: Brain cells adapt to a low-sodium environment. Pulling water out of them too quickly damages the myelin, causing permanent neurologic injury. Sodium is raised slowly and deliberately.

concepts.title: Hematologic: Clotting basics, DIC and HIT

questions.question: The first responders to a blood vessel injury are:
choices: Platelets, which stick to the injury and form a plug
questions.explanation: Platelets adhere and clump at the site within seconds. The clotting cascade then lays down fibrin to reinforce that plug into a stable clot.

questions.question: PT/INR and aPTT measure:
choices: How long the clotting cascade takes to form fibrin
questions.explanation: These are timing tests of the coagulation proteins. Warfarin prolongs PT/INR; heparin prolongs aPTT. Neither tells you anything about platelet number.

questions.question: In DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), why do patients bleed AND clot?
choices: Widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors, leaving none to stop bleeding
questions.explanation: A trigger (sepsis, trauma, obstetric emergencies) activates clotting everywhere. Tiny clots block vessels while factors and platelets are consumed, so the patient oozes from every site.

questions.question: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is dangerous mainly because of:
choices: New clots forming despite a falling platelet count
questions.explanation: HIT is an immune reaction that activates platelets. The count drops because platelets are being consumed in clots — so the treatment is to stop heparin and start a different anticoagulant, not to transfuse platelets.

questions.question: Sepsis is best understood as:
choices: A dysregulated body response to infection that damages the body's own organs
questions.explanation: The infection starts it, but the harm comes from the body's exaggerated inflammatory response — leaky vessels, vasodilation, microclots, and failing organs.

questions.question: Septic shock is sepsis plus:
choices: Low blood pressure needing vasopressors and elevated lactate despite fluids
questions.explanation: Shock means perfusion is failing. In septic shock, fluids alone can't keep MAP up and lactate stays elevated — markers that cells are not getting enough oxygen.

questions.question: Why is lactate measured in suspected sepsis?
choices: It rises when tissues aren't getting enough oxygen
questions.explanation: Under-perfused cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and make lactate. A high or rising lactate flags hidden shock even when blood pressure looks okay; a falling lactate suggests resuscitation is working.

questions.question: The single most time-sensitive sepsis intervention is:
choices: Antibiotics given promptly after cultures are drawn
questions.explanation: Every hour of delay in effective antibiotics is associated with higher mortality. Cultures are drawn first when it doesn't delay treatment, then antibiotics go in fast.

questions.question: After fluids, the first-line vasopressor for septic shock is:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine mostly constricts vessels to restore tone with less tachycardia than dopamine, which is why guidelines recommend it first.

questions.question: 'Autonomy' in healthcare ethics means:
choices: Doing what is best for the patient
The patient's right to make their own informed decisions
questions.explanation: Autonomy is self-determination. A competent patient may refuse treatment even when clinicians disagree, as long as the decision is informed.

questions.question: 'Beneficence' and 'non-maleficence' mean, respectively:
choices: Do good, and do no harm
questions.explanation: Beneficence is acting for the patient's benefit; non-maleficence is avoiding harm. Many ICU dilemmas are a tension between these and the patient's own wishes.

questions.question: A DNR (do-not-resuscitate) order means:
choices: No CPR if the heart stops — all other care continues unless otherwise specified
questions.explanation: DNR addresses one thing: resuscitation at cardiac arrest. Antibiotics, fluids, surgery, and symptom management may all still be given unless the plan says otherwise.

questions.question: When a patient can't speak for themselves, the surrogate's decision should be based on:
choices: What the patient would have wanted (substituted judgment)
questions.explanation: The surrogate's role is to be the patient's voice — using an advance directive or prior conversations. Only if the patient's wishes are unknown does 'best interest' guide the choice.

questions.question: Palliative care is:
choices: Only for the last days of life
Symptom relief and support that can be given alongside curative treatment
questions.explanation: Palliative care focuses on comfort and quality of life at any stage of serious illness, and can run in parallel with aggressive treatment. Hospice is a subset for patients near the end of life.
